sources.title: LeetCode 1047 Remove All Adjacent Duplicates In String

claims.text: The preserved interview source asks for in-place adjacent-duplicate removal, explicitly references LeetCode 1047, and asks to compare stack and two-pointer time/space; the official 1047 statement defines repeated removal of adjacent equal lowercase letters, unique final output, and length up to 100000.

Java SE 21 String values cannot be changed after creation, so true in-place overwrite applies to a mutable character buffer; a String wrapper must obtain mutable storage and construct a returned String.

OpenJDK 21 validation confirms both implementations on official examples, cascading and repeated-character boundaries, 1000 deterministic random cases versus an independent repeated-removal oracle, and length-100000 boundaries.

findings: The answer stays on the exact repository source: LeetCode 1047 adjacent-pair removal plus explicit stack-versus-two-pointer complexity comparison.
The candidate separates algorithmic auxiliary space on an already mutable char buffer from end-to-end Java String allocation, avoiding the common false O(1)-total-space claim.
The stack and two-pointer implementations preserve the same push/pop invariant; the latter reuses the input buffer prefix rather than allocating a separate state buffer.
OpenJDK 21 validation covers official examples, cascading cancellation, maximum-length boundaries, and 1000 deterministic random cases checked against an independent repeated-removal oracle.
The answer keeps lowercase-English-letter and Java String immutability boundaries explicit and does not fabricate production experience.
